clue.text: Young mother's introductory claim sadly true

parts.note: a mother introducing herself might say 'I'm Ma'

indicators.note: sadly suggests the letters of the word true are knocked out of shape and rearranged

explanation.surface: A young mother makes an opening claim that turns out, regrettably, to be accurate.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a mother claiming something; the trick is that the claim is the self-introduction 'I'm Ma', and 'sadly' signals the rearranged letters that follow it.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone young is not yet fully grown or developed, the core sense of the adjective.

clue.text: Sample book card player has to pay attention to

parts.note: in bridge the four players are North, East, South and West, so S is a player
to watch something is to pay attention to it

explanation.surface: A card player must keep an eye on a book of samples.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has to' is only a link. S for South is a bridge player, a standard crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: A bound set of fabric or colour samples is called by this name, as is a single sample.

clue.text: After changes, tries informing English politician

indicators.note: after changes means once the letters of tries informing have been shuffled about

explanation.surface: A politician, after a reshuffle, tries his hand at informing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After changes' rearranges the letters of TRIES INFORMING plus E into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The minister in charge of a country's relations with other nations is a senior politician.

clue.text: The writer's having flower within grasp

indicators.note: within places the flower inside the writer's word

parts.note: the writer refers to the setter, so the writer's is my
an aster is a daisy-like flower

explanation.surface: An author holds a bloom in hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having' is only a link word; 'The writer's' is the setter speaking of himself, a standard crossword convention.
explanation.definitionFit: A firm grasp of a subject is complete command or skill in it.

clue.text: Construction books missing from deficient supply

indicators.note: supply read as 'supplely', bending the leftover letters into a new order
missing from tells us to take the letters for books out of the word deficient

parts.note: NT stands for New Testament, a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A building project is short of materials, with books absent from a meagre stock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'missing from' removes NT from DEFICIENT, leaving DEFICIE; 'supply' (read as supple-ly) rearranges that into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A large imposing building is a construction in the sense of something built.

clue.text: Body parts some teachers aspire to?

parts.note: heads and a hip are both parts of the body
heads and a hip are both parts of the body

explanation.surface: A question about which bits of the body ambitious teachers hope to reach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Body parts' gives two pieces, HEADS and HIP; the question mark flags the playful definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The post of head teacher is the promotion many teachers aim for in their careers.

clue.text: Son filling belly with old relish

indicators.note: filling means the son's letter goes inside the word for belly

parts.note: gut is another word for belly

explanation.surface: A boy fills his stomach with old pickle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'filling' puts S inside GUT; O follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something with gusto means with great enjoyment or zest, a synonym of relish.

clue.text: Angry, extremely hostile sheep

indicators.note: extremely takes the extreme ends, first and last letters, of hostile

parts.note: a tup is a ram, a male sheep

explanation.surface: A ram is described as angry and fiercely aggressive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' gives the ends of HOSTILE, H and E. TUP is a British dialect word for a ram.
explanation.definitionFit: Being worked up and agitated is an informal idiom for being angry.

clue.text: Syndicate staff installing current power source

parts.note: a ring is a group or cartel working together

indicators.note: installing means the staff word takes the current inside it

parts.note: to man something is to staff it
I is the symbol for electric current

explanation.surface: A business group's workers fit an electrical supply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'installing' puts I inside MAN. A ring main is the British domestic circuit feeding the wall sockets.
explanation.definitionFit: A loop of household wiring supplies the electricity to the sockets in British homes.

clue.text: Briefest check on bad egg

indicators.note: in an across clue, on means placed after

parts.note: a cur is a contemptible person, a bad egg
a test is a check

explanation.surface: A very short inspection of a rotten egg.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'on' means placed after; 'bad egg' is a dated British phrase for a rotten person.
explanation.definitionFit: The superlative of curt, meaning most abrupt and short, matches briefest.

clue.text: Good meat with new stuffing, just the thing

indicators.note: stuffing means new goes inside the meat, like stuffing in a joint

parts.note: beef is a meat
it means just the right thing, as in 'that's it'

explanation.surface: Fine meat stuffed with something fresh is exactly what is needed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good' is a noun here, as in 'for your own good'. 'stuffing' puts N inside BEEF.
explanation.definitionFit: A benefit is an advantage, the noun sense of good as in the common good.

clue.text: Trace of gold in base metal under discussion — it shouldn't be put in case

definitions.text: it shouldn't be put in case

parts.note: lead is a base, non-precious metal

indicators.note: in places the trace of gold inside the phrase for under discussion

parts.note: a matter in question is under discussion

indicators.note: a trace of a word is just its first letter

explanation.surface: A hint of gold in a lesser metal is being debated, though it shouldn't be packed away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'case' is a court case: counsel examining their own witness must not ask questions that suggest the desired reply.
explanation.definitionFit: A question that prompts the desired reply is improper for a lawyer questioning their own witness in court.

clue.text: Display of nerves from daughter, one of two heading off

indicators.note: heading off removes the first letter of the word for one of two

parts.note: either means one or other of two

explanation.surface: A daughter shows nervousness as one of two people sets off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading off' removes the first letter; 'from' is only a link. The definition is a noun, as in 'all of a dither'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in a state of nervous indecision is a noun sense, as in being all of a flutter.

clue.text: Shred next file, removing the odd formal item

parts.note: a whit is a tiny bit, a shred

indicators.note: removing the odd letters keeps only the even-placed letters of next file

explanation.surface: Destroy the next document, discarding the strange one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'removing the odd' drops N, X, F, L from NEXT FILE, leaving ETIE.
explanation.definitionFit: A dress code of tailcoat and bow tie, the most formal evening wear, is named after its neckwear.

clue.text: Dope almost leading to a good lord's dishonour

indicators.note: almost means the word for dope loses its last letter

parts.note: dope is slang for information
my and good lord are both exclamations of surprise; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: Drugs nearly ruin a nobleman's good name.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims INFO to INF; then A and MY (as in 'oh my!').
explanation.definitionFit: Infamy is notoriety and public disgrace, which is a state of dishonour.

clue.text: Steersman's crash the cause of false alarm?

indicators.note: a crash wrecks the steersman's letters, which are reassembled

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: A helmsman's crash set off an alarm that turned out to be false.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crash' rearranges STEERSMANS.
explanation.definitionFit: This phrase means an illusory discovery or a hoax, something that raises excitement for nothing.

clue.text: Back trouble nurse gets to grips with

indicators.note: gets to grips with means the nurse word grasps the trouble word inside it

parts.note: to tend is to nurse
to ail is to trouble

explanation.surface: A nurse tackles a sufferer's backache.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back' looks like a body part with 'trouble' as backache, but it means the rear end of something.
explanation.definitionFit: The rear or final part of something, such as a procession, is its back.

clue.text: Gangling youth leader contacted first

indicators.note: first means the contacted word comes before the youth leader

parts.note: rang means telephoned, contacted

indicators.note: the leader of youth is its first letter

explanation.surface: A lanky youth leader was the first to be phoned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leader' gives Y; 'first' puts RANG ahead of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Tall, thin and long-limbed describes both words, a close synonym.

clue.text: The speaker's making a gesture and resigning

indicators.note: the speaker's version means the word as heard, not as spelt

parts.note: waving is making a gesture with the hand

explanation.surface: A speaker gestures while quitting office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The speaker's' signals a word that sounds like WAVING.
explanation.definitionFit: To waive is to give up or relinquish a right, much as resigning gives up a claim.

clue.text: One's to express disapproval after upsetting African people

indicators.note: after means the disapproval word comes first, with the upset piece following it

parts.note: to tut is to click the tongue in disapproval

indicators.note: upsetting in a down clue turns the letters upside down, so read backwards

parts.note: one's read as 'one is', giving I and IS

explanation.surface: Someone tuts disapprovingly after upsetting an African community.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's' must be read as 'I is', giving IS; 'upsetting' in a down clue turns it over to SI.
explanation.definitionFit: A Bantu people of Rwanda and Burundi in central Africa bear this name.

clue.text: Drug belt for Arab carrier, perhaps

parts.note: horse is slang for heroin
to belt is to hit, as is to box

explanation.surface: A narcotic strapped to someone carrying it for an Arab.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' is a link. The Arab is the horse breed, which travels in this trailer.
explanation.definitionFit: A trailer or van carries horses, and an Arab is a breed of horse, hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Very subtle witticism following penalties

indicators.note: following means the witticism comes after the penalties

parts.note: fines are monetary penalties
a pun is a play on words, a witticism

explanation.surface: A clever quip comes after the fines are handed out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'following' means placed after. 'Very subtle' is figurative: literally the word means spun extremely thin.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally spun very thin, it figuratively means delicate or overly subtle.

clue.text: Something you shouldn't ask a woman? It's accepted tradition

indicators.note: accepted means the it is taken in inside the phrase

parts.words: Something you shouldn't ask a woman?
parts.note: etiquette says never ask a woman her age
it, with 's for is joining it to the indicator

explanation.surface: A question one should not put to a woman, as convention has it.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful definition-by-example of the outer piece; 'accepted' means taken in.
explanation.definitionFit: Customs and values passed down through generations form an inheritance, a tradition.

clue.text: Scrooge film cast refusing G and T

parts.note: a skin is a thin film covering something

indicators.note: refusing G and T means the G is turned away in favour of T

parts.note: to fling is to cast or throw

explanation.surface: A film adaptation of Dickens's miser, with the actors declining a gin and tonic.
explanation.walkthrough: 'refusing G and T' swaps the G in FLING for T, giving FLINT. G and T looks like the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Dickens's Scrooge is the archetypal miser, and a mean person is called this.

clue.text: Restrained Society journalist left his boss

parts.note: a hack is a journalist
the journalist's boss is the editor, ED

explanation.surface: A society reporter departed, holding back his editor.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces simply follow in clue order.
explanation.definitionFit: Being put in chains holds a person back, literally restraining them.

clue.text: It's presumed establishment hasn't succeeded

indicators.note: hasn't means the establishment word lacks the letter for succeeded

parts.note: premises are the building of a business, an establishment

explanation.surface: Assumptions that a business has failed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hasn't' removes one S from PREMISES.
explanation.definitionFit: A proposition taken as given at the start of an argument is something presumed.

clue.text: Guards note topsy-turvy way of thinking

parts.note: to mind is to guard, so minds means guards

indicators.note: topsy-turvy in a down clue turns the note upside down, read backwards

parts.note: te is a note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: Sentries take a note of a muddled outlook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'topsy-turvy' turns TE into ET.
explanation.definitionFit: A fixed set of attitudes is a habitual way of thinking.

clue.text: Expert carries a lot of weight now

indicators.note: carries means the expert word holds the weight inside it

parts.note: an ace is an expert
a ton is a large weight

explanation.surface: A skilled lifter bears a heavy load right away.
explanation.walkthrough: A ton is a British unit of weight; 'carries' signals one piece holding another.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something immediately means doing it without delay, right now.

clue.text: Cook one way shortly before another

indicators.note: shortly means the road word is cut short by its last letter

parts.note: a road is a way
ST, street, is another way

explanation.surface: A cook takes one route quickly before trying a different one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shortly' trims the last letter; 'before' is only a link. ST, street, is another kind of way.
explanation.definitionFit: To cook meat in an oven by dry heat is a common sense of the verb.

clue.text: Changing sides in skirmish, look embarrassed

indicators.note: changing sides swaps right for left inside the skirmish word

parts.note: a brush is a brief encounter or skirmish

explanation.surface: Switching allegiance during a fight, someone appears red-faced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Changing sides in' swaps R (right) for L (left) in BRUSH.
explanation.definitionFit: Going red in the face is the outward sign of feeling embarrassed.
